explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The LORD delivered Israel into the hand of the Philistines for forty years (Judges 13:1). Forty YEARS. I thought my stretch in a junk drawer felt long, and I at least had a twist tie to talk to.

Close, baker, because Israel did face the Ammonites earlier. Jephthah crossed over to fight them (Judges 11:32). But in this passage, the LORD delivers Israel into the hand of the Philistines for forty years (Judges 13:1). Same Israel, new trouble.

The Midianites are from an earlier chapter, friend. Back in Gideon's day, the LORD gave Israel into the hand of Midian for seven years (Judges 6:1). This time it's different: He delivers them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years (Judges 13:1). Check the batch label before you stamp, baker.

explanations.answer: She will conceive and give birth to a son
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The angel says, "…you will conceive and give birth to a son." (Judges 13:3). Picture it. Somebody tells you the hard thing is true, and then in the very same breath says, "But watch this." That's a good turn in a story.

explanations.answer: She will care for an orphan from her clan
explanations.explanation: I see why a kind answer like that tempts you, friend. But the angel never mentions an orphan. He says she will "…conceive and give birth to a son." (Judges 13:3). Her own child, coming her way.

explanations.answer: She will live to see Israel set free
explanations.explanation: That one jumps way ahead, baker. The angel says nothing here about what she will live to see. What he says is that she will "…conceive and give birth to a son." (Judges 13:3). The freedom talk comes after, and it's about the boy (Judges 13:5).

explanations.answer: Begin to set Israel free from them
explanations.explanation: Right on, friend. The angel says the boy "…will begin the deliverance of Israel from the hand of the Philistines." (Judges 13:5). Notice the word "begin." He starts the job, and the angel doesn't say he finishes it.

explanations.answer: Make peace between Israel and them
explanations.explanation: Peace talks would be a nice batch, baker, but that's not on the order. The angel says the boy "…will begin the deliverance of Israel from the hand of the Philistines." (Judges 13:5). Deliverance means getting out from under their hand. The word peace never shows up in that promise.

explanations.answer: Rule over Israel as its king
explanations.explanation: That's a big crown to hand a baby who isn't even born, friend. The angel never says king. He says the boy "…will begin the deliverance of Israel from the hand of the Philistines." (Judges 13:5). Same boy, different job.

True, baker. She says, "I did not ask him where he came from, and he did not tell me his name." (Judges 13:6). She also says his appearance was like the angel of God, "exceedingly awesome." A visitor that awesome, and no name tag.

I'd check that one again, friend. The woman tells her husband, "I did not ask him where he came from, and he did not tell me his name." (Judges 13:6). So no name was given. The text says it plainly, and she's the one who tells it to Manoah.

Sharp eyes, baker! When she repeats it, she tells him about the wine, the strong drink and the unclean food (Judges 13:7). She also says the boy will be a Nazirite to God. But the part about no razor touching his head isn't in her retelling.

Read her words one more time, friend. In Judges 13:7, she mentions wine, strong drink, unclean food and the Nazirite promise. The razor line from the angel (Judges 13:5) isn't in what she says. She does add that he'll be a Nazirite "…until the day of his death."

Yes, baker. Manoah prays, "…let the man of God You sent us come to us again to teach us how to raise the boy who is to be born." (Judges 13:8). He hasn't even met the baby yet and he's already asking for the lesson. I wish more of us would ask for instructions BEFORE the dough's in the oven.

Naming comes later, friend. Manoah's prayer is about how to "…raise the boy who is to be born." (Judges 13:8). The name gets picked once the baby arrives, when the woman gives birth to a son and names him Samson (Judges 13:24).

Protect is a good dad word, baker, but it isn't the one he prays. Manoah asks for the man of God to come again "…to teach us how to raise the boy who is to be born." (Judges 13:8). He's asking for teaching.

Not quite, friend. The angel of God returns to the woman as she sits in the field, "but her husband Manoah was not with her." (Judges 13:9). Manoah prayed for this visit, and he's somewhere else when it happens. Sometimes the answer comes while you're out getting the mail.

That's it, baker. Judges 13:9 says the angel of God returned to the woman as she was sitting in the field, "but her husband Manoah was not with her." The same verse says God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel returned. His prayer got answered, and he missed the front-row seat.

explanations.answer: She runs quickly to tell her husband
explanations.explanation: That's what she does, friend. "The woman ran quickly to tell her husband…" (Judges 13:10). She doesn't walk it and she doesn't wait. Good news makes people move, and I've seen a lot of bakers run to the oven when it smells right.

explanations.answer: She asks the angel to come home with her
explanations.explanation: I can see her wanting to, baker, but the text doesn't say that. It says she "…ran quickly to tell her husband…" (Judges 13:10). She goes for Manoah, and he follows her back.

explanations.answer: She sends a servant to find Manoah
explanations.explanation: No servant in this scene, friend. The text says the woman herself "…ran quickly to tell her husband…" (Judges 13:10). She carries the news with her own feet. Some news you don't hand off to a messenger, and I think this was one of those.

True, baker. Manoah asks, "Are you the man who spoke to my wife?" and the man answers, "I am" (Judges 13:11). A short answer, and it's all Manoah needs to hear. I'd say that's a man who knows his facts.
Not this time, friend. When Manoah asks if he's the man who spoke to his wife, the man says, "I am" (Judges 13:11). So he owns it right away. No dodging, and no hunting for a side door.

explanations.answer: His wife must do all the angel told her
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The angel of the LORD answers, "Your wife is to do everything I told her." (Judges 13:13). Then he repeats it in the next verse: "She must do everything I have commanded her." (Judges 13:14). Manoah asked a big question and got a plain, clear answer.

explanations.answer: Manoah must take the boy to the priests
explanations.explanation: Priests never come up in this answer, friend. The angel of the LORD says, "Your wife is to do everything I told her." (Judges 13:13). He points Manoah back to what he already told her.

explanations.answer: Manoah must teach the boy to fight
explanations.explanation: That's a fun guess, baker, but the angel doesn't say it. His answer is, "Your wife is to do everything I told her." (Judges 13:13). Nothing about fighting lessons in that reply.

True, friend. The angel says, "She must not eat anything that comes from the vine, nor drink any wine or strong drink, nor eat anything unclean." (Judges 13:14). The vine is new in that list, since the first time the angel spoke he mentioned wine, strong drink and unclean food (Judges 13:4). And he ends with, "She must do everything I have commanded her."

Look at the verse again, baker. The angel of the LORD says, "She must not eat anything that comes from the vine, nor drink any wine or strong drink, nor eat anything unclean." (Judges 13:14). The vine part is right there. It gets added to what he said the first time (Judges 13:4).

explanations.answer: They should offer it up instead
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The angel says, "Even if I stay, I will not eat your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD." (Judges 13:16). So an offering is for the LORD, not for the angel's plate. Manoah wanted to host a guest, and the angel points him to the LORD instead.

explanations.answer: He will gladly stay and eat it
explanations.explanation: I bet that's what Manoah was hoping, friend, but the angel says otherwise. "Even if I stay, I will not eat your food." (Judges 13:16). Then he adds, "But if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD." So that goat is not going on the angel's plate.

explanations.answer: They should save it for the birth
explanations.explanation: Nice planning, baker, but nobody mentions a birth party here. The angel says, "Even if I stay, I will not eat your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD." (Judges 13:16). The goat is headed to the LORD.

Not this time, friend. The angel of the LORD answers Manoah's question with a question: "Why do you ask my name, since it is beyond comprehension?" (Judges 13:18). Manoah asked, and no name came back. The text says the angel's name is beyond comprehension.

That's right, baker. Manoah asks for a name, and the angel of the LORD says, "Why do you ask my name, since it is beyond comprehension?" (Judges 13:18). So Manoah walks away without a name. Honestly, I'd have asked twice.

Yes, baker. "When the flame went up from the altar to the sky, the angel of the LORD ascended in the flame." (Judges 13:20). The text says the LORD did a marvelous thing, and Manoah and his wife looked on as it happened. When they saw it, they fell facedown to the ground. That's a visit nobody forgets.

Not quite, friend. This verse has the angel going somewhere: "…the angel of the LORD ascended in the flame." (Judges 13:20). The flame goes up from the altar to the sky, and he goes up in it. Manoah and his wife look on while it happens.

He'd already done plenty of speaking by then, baker. In this verse, the flame goes up from the altar to the sky, and "…the angel of the LORD ascended in the flame." (Judges 13:20). Manoah and his wife watch it happen.

True, friend. "When Manoah and his wife saw this, they fell facedown to the ground." (Judges 13:20). They go down right after the flame goes up and the angel ascends in it. Both of them, and straight down. I've dropped to the floor myself, mostly when I've dropped a whole tray of dough.

Check that verse, baker. It says, "When Manoah and his wife saw this, they fell facedown to the ground." (Judges 13:20). They don't run and they don't stand there staring. They go facedown, both of them.

That's what he says, baker. "We are going to die…" he tells his wife, "for we have seen God!" (Judges 13:22). I think that came out fast and shaky. That's a man whose heart has just caught up with what his eyes saw.

explanations.answer: We must go after the angel
explanations.explanation: Chasing him down is a reasonable idea, friend, but Manoah doesn't say it. The angel has already gone up in the flame, and Manoah says, "We are going to die, for we have seen God!" (Judges 13:22). His mind goes somewhere much heavier.

explanations.answer: We must tell all of Zorah
explanations.explanation: Spreading the news is what a lot of us would do, baker, but Manoah doesn't say it here. His words to his wife are, "We are going to die, for we have seen God!" (Judges 13:22). Zorah is his hometown (Judges 13:2), and there's no word of telling the neighbors yet.

Yes, baker. Manoah's wife says, "If the LORD had intended to kill us, He would not have accepted the burnt offering and the grain offering from our hands…" (Judges 13:23). She goes on to say He wouldn't have shown them all these things or spoken to them this way. Manoah brought fear, and I think she brought a calm look at what had actually happened.

explanations.answer: The angel promised them long life
explanations.explanation: That promise isn't in this story, friend. His wife points to what the LORD had done: "…He would not have accepted the burnt offering and the grain offering from our hands…" (Judges 13:23). Her reasons come from what happened that day.

explanations.answer: They obeyed every rule he gave
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason she gives, baker. She says, "If the LORD had intended to kill us, He would not have accepted the burnt offering and the grain offering from our hands…" (Judges 13:23). Her reasoning rests on what the LORD had accepted, shown and spoken.

That's the one, friend. "…the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him at Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol." (Judges 13:25). The boy grew, the LORD blessed him, and then the Spirit began to stir. The word "began" tells me something is just getting started.

Manoah did ask a lot of good questions, baker, but this verse isn't about his words. It says, "…the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him at Mahaneh-dan…" (Judges 13:25). The stirring comes from the LORD's Spirit.

No dreams in this verse, friend. The text says, "…the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him at Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol." (Judges 13:25). Nothing here is something Samson sees in his sleep. The stirring comes from the Spirit of the LORD, and I think that's a much better wake-up call than any alarm clock.
